query: How does the eval maturity progression determine when a team should introduce LLM-as-judge grading, and what setup cost does that grading approach require before it produces trustworthy scores?
expected_answer: LLM-as-judge is rung 3 in the four-rung eval ladder (manual review, golden-set grading, LLM-judge, user feedback), introduced around week 4+ of refining once golden-set failures reveal quality criteria—like tone or completeness—that heuristic grading can't express, and it runs via `make eval-gate` in CI. Before those scores mean anything, the judge needs calibration: writing 3-5 quality criteria, creating 5-10 human-graded sample outputs, writing a judge prompt, and running the judge on the samples until it agrees with human grades. Because the judge is non-deterministic and costs money per run, the recommendation is to run cheap heuristic golden-set grading in CI and reserve LLM-judge for on-demand quality audits rather than a per-PR gate.

query: In eval-driven development, why does the eval suite have to exist before tuning starts, and how does that relate to sizing the golden set at spec time versus after launch?
expected_answer: EDD requires authoring the behavioral case set before the agent can satisfy it, because every tuning change is a global change—a prompt tweak that fixes three failures can silently break four others, so with only a handful of cases you'd see the fixes and miss the regressions and ship anyway. This is why the golden set only needs to be small (20-50 cases) at discovery-exit/initial spec time: it exists to define planned capabilities honestly before the agent exists, not to catch every regression yet. The set is meant to grow toward CI-scale numbers (100-1,000) only after launch, fed by real production failures, rather than being over-specced as a genesis-time obligation.

query: Why is scoring an agent on pass^k over multiple trials still not enough to trust that agent, and what does trajectory-level evaluation catch that even a multi-trial outcome metric misses?
expected_answer: Pass^k measures whether all k trials succeed, and it falls sharply as k rises—a 75% per-trial success rate only passes three consecutive trials about 42% of the time—which already shows raw per-trial pass rates flatter agents run unattended or facing users who need reliability every time. But pass^k, like any outcome metric, still only scores the final answer over repeated samples; it can't detect a 'lucky trajectory,' such as an agent that got the right answer via a wrong tool route or a retry that discarded correct evidence it had already retrieved. Trajectory evaluation catches these by scoring individual nodes (routing choice, whether retry evidence survived, whether escalation fired correctly) as deterministic, mechanically checkable assertions—failures invisible to any outcome-based metric, no matter how many trials it runs.

query: How does the eval harness's routing-accuracy suite map onto Anthropic's three-tier eval taxonomy, and what score floor does it enforce in CI?
expected_answer: The eval harness's routing accuracy suite corresponds to Tier 2 (trajectory evals) in Anthropic's taxonomy—it checks whether the agent routes to the right domain/subagent, analogous to asserting the ordered list of nodes/tools visited, and it's implemented via the `tool_trajectory_avg_score` metric (exact match on tool name and args, 1.0 = perfect). The harness explicitly cites the Anthropic three-tier taxonomy as the framework underlying its four suites. In CI, `make eval-routing eval-behavioral` runs with a routing score floor of 0.85 and a behavioral floor of 0.90 (`check_floor.py`), failing the build if routing drops below that threshold to catch prompt/routing regressions before production.

query: If an eval's pass rate drops, why shouldn't that be treated as a code test failure, and what debugging order does the maintenance discipline prescribe before touching the agent itself?
expected_answer: Tests and evals are different instruments: a test failing means the code is wrong (deterministic assertion, always a bug), while an eval score dropping means something moved—prompt, model, data, or code—and could be noise rather than a real regression, since evals measure a pass rate over a set against a threshold rather than an exact match. Because of this ambiguity, the maintenance discipline says never assume the agent got worse first: check infrastructure errors/timeouts, then inspect failed traces and grader decisions, then check whether failures concentrate in one task category, and only then modify the model, prompt, tools, or agent logic. Skipping straight to step 4 means tuning a real agent against a broken measurement, which can make the number improve while the agent actually gets worse.

query: Both the RAG cross-encoder reranker and the LightGBM/CatBoost playlist reranker produce scores meant to be compared on a consistent scale—what mechanism does each use to get there, and why does that matter for downstream use of the score?
expected_answer: The RAG cross-encoder reranker (`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`) produces unbounded raw logits per (query, chunk) pair and applies a sigmoid to map them into a consistent [0,1] range, which is what lets the CRAG confidence gate compare `max(relevance_score)` against a fixed threshold. The LightGBM/CatBoost comparison instead evaluates whether GBM outputs are well-calibrated probabilities usable directly as a rerank score, using Brier score and log-loss rather than AUC—because a miscalibrated-but-well-ranked model still produces unusable absolute scores. Both cases treat calibration (not just ranking accuracy) as the property that makes a reranker's score safe to threshold or compare downstream.

query: When a copilot agent implements episodic memory using LangGraph's cross-thread store, what write-timing tradeoff should it make, and how does that store's data differ in kind from what the checkpointer holds?
expected_answer: Episodic memory (past conversation summaries per user) is implemented via BaseStore, which persists data across threads, unlike the checkpointer which only holds full state snapshots for a single thread. For write timing, background writes (an async task spawned after the run completes) are preferred for episodic session summaries since they add no latency, versus hot-path writes which are only justified when the memory is needed within the same run (e.g. a procedural update affecting the current response). Implementation-wise, this costs about one Haiku call per session (~$0.0001) and is considered high ROI since it enables 'last time you asked about X' recall.

query: How does Memoria's exponential decay scoring avoid needing the explicit conflict-resolution step that memory lifecycle theory says is required for a true memory system, and what does that tradeoff cost?
expected_answer: Memory lifecycle theory holds that a store which only appends facts (like both 'user is vegetarian' and 'user ordered steak') has no way to know which is current — that's a log, not memory, and stage E (update/forget) requires detecting the contradiction to resolve it. Memoria's decay weighting sidesteps this: it scores every memory by recency (w = e^(-alpha*age), min-max normalized so ranking reflects relative age within the retrieved set) so the newer fact simply outranks the older one at read time, without anything ever noticing they conflict. The cost is that stable, durable facts decay at the same rate as volatile ones, so a preference stated once and never contradicted will eventually rank below noise — the usual fix is a two-tier design with a small always-injected profile for durable facts and decay applied only to the episodic layer beneath it.

query: What specific message-count parameters does the LangGraph summarization node use, and how does that concrete implementation map onto the general compaction pipeline's retention priorities?
expected_answer: The LangGraph summarization node fires when message history reaches an 8-message trigger threshold, summarizes the older messages with Haiku, and retains the last 4 messages verbatim as overlap, replacing the summarized portion with a single SystemMessage. This maps directly onto the general compaction pipeline's principle that recent turns must be preserved verbatim (since the agent's immediate working state lives there) while older reasoning gets summarized — the node's 4-message overlap is a concrete instance of that 'preserve recent messages verbatim' retention step, and its use of a separate cheap model (Haiku) reflects treating the summarization step as lossy-but-bounded compression of the middle of the conversation.

query: Why does 'context rot' happen even when a fact is verbatim present in the window, and which failure mode in the broader failure taxonomy is this, versus the one caused by high volume of merely plausible content?
expected_answer: Context rot happens because attention is a fixed budget divided across n-squared pairwise token relationships in a transformer — adding tokens doesn't expand capacity, it thins attention across more claimants, so exact-match retrieval of a planted fact degrades as filler increases even though the fact is unmodified and present. In the context failure-modes taxonomy, this is 'Rot' (occupancy grows, recall degrades, correct earlier in a session but wrong later) — distinct from 'Distraction,' where attention drifts to individually plausible but marginal content (e.g. retrieving 40 relevant-ish documents when only 3 answer the question), which is a volume-of-plausible-content problem rather than an attention-thinning-with-occupancy problem.

query: Why must a timestamp never be placed at the top of a system prompt, and what ordering rule for the rest of the window follows from the same underlying caching mechanism?
expected_answer: Prompt caching works by exact-match prefix matching on Claude's KV cache, so a timestamp at the top of the system prompt breaks byte-identity on every call and destroys cache reuse for the entire window, forcing full-prefix reprocessing (~100% token cost) instead of only paying for the novel suffix (~10%). This is why context should be ordered stable-before-dynamic: system prompt, tools, and stable memory form the static cacheable prefix, while retrieved docs, history, and runtime state (which change per call) go after it, with the current query last — runtime injection like date/time belongs in a dynamic layer assembled programmatically rather than baked into the cached prefix.

query: Why can't prompt injection be fully fixed with in-context defences, and what is the one layered defence against it that actually provides a guarantee rather than a probability?
expected_answer: Injection can't be fully fixed at the prompt layer because LLMs process instructions and data in the same channel with no structural separation — an attacker's text has no principled marker distinguishing it from a legitimate instruction, so defences like structural delimiting, trust zones, and instruction hierarchy are all probabilistic and can in principle be talked around. The context-failure-modes taxonomy identifies code-level enforcement as the load-bearing exception: a permission hook or other code-level control cannot be talked out of denying a write, unlike every context-level defence, which is why architectures should assume injection eventually succeeds and bound impact via things like least privilege and egress control rather than trying to prevent it outright.

query: When a RAG API endpoint sends multiple query reformulations to the retrieval graph in parallel, how does RRF's cross-query consensus fusion relate to the global deduplication step the API applies before returning results?
expected_answer: The RAG API design pattern runs 2-3 LLM-generated query variants through the retrieval graph in parallel via asyncio.gather, then merges and globally deduplicates results by chunk_id or content fingerprint (highest score wins) before returning them in the typed QueryResponse. RRF is the fusion mechanism that should occur upstream of that dedup step: it merges the multiple ranked lists from BM25, dense, and multi-query results by rank position rather than raw score, promoting chunks that multiple query variants agree on (e.g. a chunk ranked #2 in two lists beats one ranked #2 in only one list) even though the API's own dedup_global function operates on raw scores, not RRF scores. RRF's implementation preserves maxRawScore rather than the RRF score specifically so that downstream score-threshold and dedup logic like the API's continues to operate on the original cosine scale.

query: Why does a semantic cache hit save more than just retrieval time, in terms of the prefill/decode cost split of LLM inference?
expected_answer: A semantic cache hit skips embedding, retrieval, reranking, and LLM generation entirely, saving roughly 3-6 seconds and 2+ LLM calls versus running the full CRAG pipeline. Since decode (sequential, one token at a time) is the expensive phase of inference while prefill is cheap and parallel, avoiding generation calls altogether removes the costliest part of the request rather than just shortening the prompt fed into prefill. This is why the cache's config target is aggressive (hits must return in ≤500ms end-to-end) — it eliminates the decode-dominated generation step rather than merely optimizing it via levers like output-length discipline or quantization.

query: How does the confidence gate in the LangGraph CRAG pipeline's graph topology implement the retry logic's off-by-one gotcha around retry_count?
expected_answer: The LangGraph CRAG pipeline's QualityGate node compares confidence_score (from RerankerAgent) against a threshold (default 0.3 in the pipeline doc, though CRAG Retry Logic cites 0.4) and, on failure, loops back to the retrieve node with incremented retry_count rather than restarting the whole graph — a surgical mid-pipeline re-entry rather than a full LoopAgent restart. The retry logic doc details the implementation gotcha in this gate: in one production version, grade_docs increments retry_count before returning, so after the first pass retry_count is already 1, and check_sufficient only allows a retry while retry_count < 2 — meaning the gate as coded permits exactly one real retry, matching the pipeline doc's stated default of max_crag_retries=1, even though the increment-then-check ordering makes it easy to misread as allowing two retries.

query: When using the Send API to fan out to a dynamic number of parallel worker nodes, what state reducer should the shared results field use, and what happens if you leave it as the default?
expected_answer: Send dispatches a runtime-determined number of parallel branches (one per chunk, query reformulation, or tool call), each returning a partial state update, and these all complete as a single super-step that must be merged into shared state at the join node. If the target field uses the default reducer (overwrite/last-write-wins), the parallel branches will silently clobber each other's results, leaving only the final write; to correctly accumulate results from all branches, the field must instead be declared with a reducer like Annotated[list, operator.add] (or add_messages for chat message lists) so the reducer appends/merges every branch's output rather than replacing it.

query: Given the layered relationship between LangChain, LangGraph, and Deep Agents, why was ADK rejected in favor of LangGraph for Librarian's CRAG retrieval pipeline specifically, rather than being a question of which of the three layered frameworks to use?
expected_answer: The framework-selection guide frames LangChain, LangGraph, and Deep Agents as layered (foundation, orchestration, batteries-included) rather than competing, with LangGraph chosen when you need complex control flow like branching/loops (explicitly citing CRAG retry as an example) or persistent state within a session. The ADK vs LangGraph decision doc explains that ADK sits outside this LangChain-family stack entirely and was rejected because its LoopAgent can only restart the full condense→analyze sequence rather than model Librarian's surgical conditional back-edge into just the retrieve node, its session state is an untyped mutable dict versus LangGraph's typed LibrarianState, and Claude/Anthropic support requires an unproven LiteLLM adapter since ADK is Gemini-native — concluding the gap was vocabulary, not architecture, so a ~2-day rename-only alignment was done instead of a full port.

query: How does knowledge graph retrieval's traversal-depth error compounding relate to when GraphRAG is worth using inside an agentic RAG system?
expected_answer: Knowledge graph retrieval shows multi-hop accuracy of 53.4% versus 42.9% for vector-only, but warns that traversal depth compounds error multiplicatively — at 85% per-hop accuracy, a 5-hop traversal is only ~44% trustworthy (0.85^5) — making entity resolution the load-bearing sub-problem and bounded traversal depth a necessity rather than an optional feature. The agentic RAG advanced patterns page positions GraphRAG (entity/relationship extraction, community detection, graph traversal instead of vector search) as the right tool specifically for relationship-traversal questions like "what do all invoices for customer X have in common," explicitly warning it is overkill and adds significant pipeline complexity for simple factual lookups — the same boundary implied by the compounding-error caveat, since shallow single-hop questions don't need a graph and deep traversal must be budgeted rather than assumed reliable.

query: If I'm exposing a wiki knowledge base as an MCP server that other agents can connect to, what invariant should the tool set enforce, and how does that relate to MCP's separation of tool definitions from the agent?
expected_answer: MCP separates tool definitions from the agent so tools are served independently and discovered by the agent at runtime, rather than being baked in at construction time — the copilot just calls a tool like the librarian MCP tool without knowing the backend. Because tools become an independently deployed surface, a knowledge-serving MCP server like the Librarian's must enforce a read-only invariant: all its tools (search_wiki, read_page, list_domain, list_pages, get_domain_briefing) are read-only, with no write/append/delete tool exposed. This invariant is enforced at the tool-definition layer itself (not via a soft prompt instruction), which is exactly the kind of security-consequential rule that benefits from MCP's decoupled, versionable tool-server boundary.

query: How do the ACI concept of tool design and the context-engineering view of tools converge on the same rule for tool descriptions and error messages?
expected_answer: ACI (Agent-Computer Interface) frames tool design as an interface problem: descriptions should state when to use a tool (and when not to, to disambiguate from similar tools), and error messages should be actionable rather than raw stack traces, since ambiguity causes agents to call the wrong tool or misuse parameters. The context-engineering view arrives at the identical prescriptions from a token-budget angle: tool descriptions are 'routing logic' that must be terse because they sit permanently in the context window, and errors should be structured and actionable (e.g. {"error_code": "not_found", "is_fatal": false}) because a stack trace is 500 tokens of noise the agent can't use. Both treat tool overlap/ambiguous boundaries as the central failure to eliminate — ACI as a reasoning-failure look-alike, context engineering as wasted resident tokens.

query: Why is sub-agent isolation described as the most expensive context lever, and how does that cost show up in the Explorer/Executor role pattern used in harness orchestration?
expected_answer: Isolation is the most expensive of the four context-engineering levers because real tokens multiply across agents while cross-agent context is lost — e.g. three sub-agents spending 80k tokens each is 240k of real spend to produce 6k of visible output for the orchestrator, and the sub-agent's window is discarded (not merged) once it returns its summary. Harness orchestration's Explorer/Executor pattern is a deliberate, cheap application of that costly lever: the Explorer gets only read-only tools and runs in an isolated, disposable context on a cheaper model, so exploration noise never pollutes the orchestrator, which stays small and holds the plan. This works only because the Explorer's prompt is scoped and bounded and it returns a condensed summary rather than its full history — the same 'summary, not transcript' discipline multi-agent context describes as the mechanism that makes isolation pay off instead of just multiplying cost.

query: An agent keeps failing the same test gate after two retries — how should the harness distinguish this from an agent stuck in a doom loop of mutating the same broken solution, and what's the correct next move in each case?
expected_answer: The two-retry rule says that after two failures on the same gate, the problem is in the context or specification, not the execution — a third attempt spends money confirming what's already known, so the harness should stop retrying and instead treat the failure as a signal that the spec or provided context is wrong (this only holds if the error was already fed back as context, per the Agent Retry Taxonomy). A doom loop is a related but distinct failure — 10+ small mutations of a broken solution converging on nothing — detected via per-file edit-count tracking, and its fix is not a hard stop but a forced 'reconsider your approach' prompt that pushes the agent to re-plan rather than repair. Both are treated as harness bugs with a common design principle: past a small attempt budget, more attempts don't produce new information, so the intervention must change the agent's strategy (re-plan, or escalate) rather than let it keep repeating.

query: For a long-running agent loop, why is an iteration/budget cap alone insufficient, and how does externalizing state to files support the stall-detection and escalation mechanisms that are supposed to catch what the cap misses?
expected_answer: A cap is only a safety backstop, not a working verifier — a loop whose normal exit is hitting max_iterations has no real success check, and caps alone can't distinguish productive work from thrashing (budget cap) or silently truncate progress that was still advancing (iteration cap); only a stall detector bounds the duration of unproductive-but-varied work, and it requires progress to be observable (a changing file, a shrinking failure count). Long-horizon execution's answer is to externalize progress to files rather than keep it only in the context window, which makes the loop re-entrant and gives the stall detector something concrete to read between iterations. That same state externalization is what makes the escalation path meaningful: when the cap or stall detector fires, the run can hand off to a fresh context (or a human) with the plan file and progress log intact, rather than losing everything that lived only in a window that's about to be discarded.

query: Where does the input guardrails pipeline sit within the five-layer safeguards architecture, and why must both stay deterministic and LLM-free rather than using an LLM to check itself?
expected_answer: The 7-stage input guardrails pipeline (normalise, size check, domain classify, injection detect, PII redact, XML envelope, advisory notes) is Layer 1 of the five-layer safeguards architecture, running pre-input in under 1ms before any LLM call, ahead of the routing confidence gate (Layer 2), retrieval quality gate/CRAG (Layer 3), post-generation grounding check (Layer 4), and escalation routing (Layer 5). Both pages insist on deterministic, LLM-free checks: the guardrails pipeline argues an LLM-based guardrail can be bypassed by the same injection techniques it's meant to catch, and the safeguards architecture explicitly forbids LLM-as-judge for its Layer 4 grounding check, reserving semantic/LLM-based grounding evaluation for the offline eval pipeline rather than the hot runtime path. Layer 1 is deterministic and near-instant (<1ms) precisely so the fast, cheap, gameable-resistant checks run first, before the costlier retrieval and generation stages.

query: If an agent's memory only matters once it enters a context window, why is decay-weighted retrieval a workable way to handle contradictory memories, and what kind of memory should it not be used for?
expected_answer: Memory has no effect on a model except by entering a context window, so every memory decision is really a decision about what occupies a future window, and episodic memory that accumulates linearly rots unless it is distilled. Decay weighting scores each memory by e^(-alpha * age) at read time over min-max normalised age, so a recent 'user eats meat' outranks an old 'user is vegetarian' without any step that detects the conflict, and the full history is kept. The cost is that stable long-lived facts decay at the same rate as volatile ones, so it suits time-stamped episodic observations; durable identity facts belong in a small always-injected profile layer above the decayed store.

query: In a design for cutting cost at 1M queries a day, why does prefix caching come first among the levers, and what does a prompt have to look like before it actually benefits?
expected_answer: The walkthrough orders the levers prefix caching, then model routing, then token trimming and output caps, then a batch API, because a 1k-token system prompt over 1M calls is about 1B repeated input tokens a day. Prefix caching only pays if the prefix is byte-identical, within a roughly 5-minute TTL, and long enough for the provider (OpenAI needs a 1,024-token threshold); then it saves about 90% of prefix cost. Dynamic content is not cached, which is why in ADK a static_instruction is eligible but an instruction callable is not.

query: A default model was trained on a sample with 30% bad accounts when the real rate is 5%. Why can't its Gini tell you anything is wrong, and what does the uncorrected score do to a 5:1 cost-ratio approval cutoff?
expected_answer: Adding -2.097 to the log odds corrects the prior shift and drops the mean PD from 0.265 to 0.047, but the Gini stays at 0.480 because the shift does not change the ranking, so a ranking metric cannot reveal the miscalibration. The cost-based cutoff (approve when PD < 1/6 at a 5:1 cost ratio) is valid only for a calibrated PD. Applied to the uncorrected score it rejects 42% and costs 0.444, worse than approving everyone (0.250), while the corrected score costs 0.245.

query: When a place's raw upstream tag was being lost, why was the new subtype column guarded by a prefix-only CHECK and shipped in the same branch as its reader?
expected_answer: The kept value is a namespaced fact such as shop:books, and the CHECK validates only the prefix because the upstream vocabulary has hundreds of values and grows outside the repo's control, so an enumerated list would go stale by design while the prefix still catches a bare value or wrong separator. The column shipped with its one reader in the same branch and review because of the schema rule that every column names its reader: an audit had found four plausible, CHECK-constrained lifecycle columns on one table where only one was read, and the dead ones were wrong about the published rows. A column nothing selects is a trap rather than documentation.

query: Per-user conversion appeared to fall from 11.34% to 9.94% while per-session conversion rose. What explains the disagreement, and why does the unit of the metric matter at all?
expected_answer: The two periods ran 198 and 108 days, and a longer window gives each user more chances to return and buy, inflating the per-user rate; over equal 108-day windows it went from 9.43% to 9.94%, moving the same way as per-session (7.48% to 7.60%). More generally a metric sampled by member weights each group by its size: the mean seen by a random member is sum(s_i^2)/sum(s_i), never below the per-group mean, so with nine users at 20 sessions and one at 500 the mean is 68.0 per user but a random session belongs to a user with 372.9. So match windows and state the denominator, choosing the unit the decision is about.

query: A platform plans to ship Postgres full-text search first and pgvector later behind one endpoint. What must the vector upgrade prove, and what does the Librarian's own hybrid benchmark suggest about expecting dense retrieval alone to win?
expected_answer: The search endpoint keeps a frozen response shape (results with title, snippet, source_url, score) so consumers never rewrite, and semantic retrieval ships only if a roughly 20-question set, hand-graded before and after, shows vector beating full-text. The Librarian benchmark shows why that gate is sensible: dense-only hit rate was 45% against 50% for BM25 and 58% for hybrid RRF, with 68% once a cross-encoder reranker was added, so dense alone is not automatically the winner. RRF is rank-based and parameter-free apart from k=60, which avoids tuning weights across score distributions.

query: In the cost-leveled review ladder, what does the default level add over a mechanical review, and how do the scanner agents it dispatches divide the work and decide severity?
expected_answer: L2, the default, adds a scanner subagent and a test run to the mechanical diff-and-lint review of L1, while L3 adds the full SANYI contract audit and is restricted to a single repo. The scanners are independent single-concern agents run in parallel (correctness, safety, structure, wander always; agent-quality and contracts only when signal detection finds agent code or a SANYI.md), each with its own ID prefix and read-only tools. Severity is derived rather than chosen: for example the contracts scanner fixes merge impact by violation code (BY blocker, JY important, BN-1 suggestion), which keeps findings comparable across parallel runs.

query: How can simulation be used to test a confidence interval method, and what does it show for the Wald interval on a rare proportion?
expected_answer: A data-generating-process check simulates data from a known process, applies the method many times and reports bias, spread and coverage, which is the general test for any interval method. For a 95% interval the claim is about the procedure's long-run coverage (a simulation gave 0.948). Applied to a rare proportion with true p = 0.02 and n = 50, Wald covers the truth only 0.633 of the time against 0.920 for Wilson, and with 0 conversions in 50 Wald returns [0, 0] while Wilson gives [0, 0.0714].

query: Why do summary statistics need a plot beside them, and what chart-axis choices can make the plot itself misleading?
expected_answer: Anscombe's four datasets share the same means (9.0 and 7.5), correlation of 0.82 and fitted line (slope 0.5, intercept 3.0) yet look like a noisy line, a curve, an outlier-dragged line and a single leverage point, so the table cannot tell you the next step. A plot can still mislead: with dual y axes whoever sets the limits invents any crossing or gap, and a bar from a non-zero baseline exaggerated an 11% difference into a bar 86% taller. The fixes are aligned panels on one time axis, indexing both series to 100, and bars that start at zero.

query: What problem does each of clustered standard errors and fixed effects solve in panel or grouped data, and what does each leave unfixed?
expected_answer: Clustered standard errors fix the standard error, not the estimate: in a group-randomised example the naive SE of 0.0411 became 0.0781 clustered, and the false-positive rate fell from 27.8% to 3.5%, though with few clusters (5) about 21% of nulls were still rejected. Fixed effects fix bias from stable unit differences by using only within-unit variation, moving a pooled estimate of -1.005 to 0.472 against a true 0.5, but they absorb time-invariant regressors and leave time-varying confounders. In a panel with a persistent regressor you also cluster by unit, since coverage was 0.697 naive against 0.940 clustered.

query: In a dbt project, where does a snapshot fit relative to the staging, core and mart layers, and why can't a lost snapshot be rebuilt like an ordinary model?
expected_answer: Models follow the layer rule that each layer reads only the one before it, and because ELT keeps the raw layer as a replay point a buggy model is cheap to fix by rebuilding. A snapshot is different: it builds Type 2 history by comparing a mutable source with what it holds on each run, so it samples, changes between runs are lost, and a missed run cannot be recovered, making a missed run an incident. For that reason snapshots read sources directly with no logic in them, so a transform bug is not baked into permanent history, and the strategy (timestamp versus check, hard_deletes: invalidate) must be chosen with care.

query: If in-session skills append to an inbox that an offline consolidator empties, why is polling the inbox size a poor metric, and how should promotion be measured instead?
expected_answer: In the single-writer design, in-session skills only write to an append-only inbox and one offline consolidator is the sole process allowed to rewrite the curated files. Because the consolidator drains the inbox, a metric sampled on a schedule measures the drain: a buffer emptied to zero undercounts when polled, as the rate-metrics page notes for a growth inbox. Promotion events must instead be logged when the transform runs, so the count does not depend on when the poll happens.

query: When does the LangGraph summarisation node fire, and why does evicting the in-memory session wrapper cost little when a Postgres checkpointer is in use?
expected_answer: Summarisation triggers at 8 messages, keeps the 4 most recent verbatim and has Haiku compress the rest into a SystemMessage beginning '[Conversation summary]:'; because the summary evolves each cycle, prefix caching helps only within a session. The session wrapper dict had leaked memory and was replaced with cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=500, ttl=1800). Since the Postgres checkpointer holds the real conversation state, evicting a wrapper loses only in-flight interrupt state, not the conversation.

query: How does a backfill that synthesises review-queue rows stay safe to re-run, and why does the machine writer then leave those rows alone?
expected_answer: The unique index on (osm_type, osm_id) does not stop a rerun because manual rows use a negative sequence id, so the guard goes on the link column venue_id: read all linked ids and skip already-linked venues. The synthesised rows are marked status accepted, review_batch null, source manual_admin and tagged with a created_by ticket tag so rollback is one delete. The machine pass only writes draft or needs_review rows, enforced in the statement itself (UPDATE ... WHERE review_status IN ('draft','needs_review')), so a row in a terminal state is outside its write set and zero rows updated means a human got there first.

query: Why does a shared calendar mislabel events onto one venue, and how did the same dependence on the source row make a direct sheet insert pass a 'done when' without being served?
expected_answer: Events inherit their venue from the source row, where the source URL is UNIQUE and the venue column is NOT NULL and singular, so a shared calendar stamps all its events with one venue; 25 of 26 festivals have no single venue, and the plan refused to register shared calendars from the propose form. The same dependence bit the done-when 'a row enrichment can pick up': a direct insert met it, but the serving path default-denies rows with no source and the legal gate returns 'posture missing'. It was tightened to 'a row with a source id and a venue id' and the work fed through the existing writer (the importer).

query: After a sanitiser silently coerced enrichment fields, what second defect hit the remediation re-run, and how does that defect work?
expected_answer: Sanitize coerces enums to a fallback and never fails, and cleanEnum with no allow-list returns the fallback unconditionally, so bad values had been overwritten while the publish script never read needs_review; the remediation re-enriched 16 of 20 rows. That run hit the empty-string env override: 'VAR= cmd' makes the variable present but empty, dotenv with override:false keeps the empty shell value, and `env.VAR ?? fallback` treats '' as a value (nullish) while `if (env.VAR)` treats it as unset. Two call sites used ??, giving a no_api_key result and model: ''; the fix is || or an explicit check, plus probing the resolved config before spending.

query: If a row was enriched from starved input and its source page later gains a real description, why won't a re-crawl simply fix it, and how should the enrichment input be repaired?
expected_answer: Starvation came from feeding operator notes (provenance) as content, so both hospitality rows returned empty vibe and context tags; the fix is real descriptive input through a pure shaping function applied after the content hash so no hash is invalidated, with a dry run per vertical printing the shaped payload and parsed response. A re-crawl will not overwrite an existing row: it only adds occurrences and dates, and a real title or description change is flagged (source_content_changed), withholding the handoff. The cost is that a real page correction waits for a human, accepted because an overwrite had been renaming public URLs, hiding published rows and reverting hand corrections.

query: Why can a green make gate still reflect no quality bar for a newly added LLM-judged metric, and where does an all-ungated eval suite finally get caught?
expected_answer: CI runs eval:grade --gate with a blank judge key, so judges degrade to heuristic-only and exit 0, and a metric registered with no target is the deliberate UNGATED state (reported as UNGATED, not skipped), while a target with no metric is an error. Gate is type-check, lint, test, build and db-drift with autofix allowed, so a gate pass says nothing about a threshold nobody has measured. Zero activated targets only warns in CD (--warn-empty) and fails at the readiness audit (/deploy-check); ship then reruns the same checks strictly with no autofix so the committed diff is the reviewed diff.

query: When the first round of an outcome measure rests on click proxies, how is the benchmark holdout assigned, and why must its key never rotate?
expected_answer: The outcome ladder has only proxies: rung 1 splits the CTA click by kind (free but silent for free events), rung 2 is add-to-calendar and rung 3 is next-day self-reported attendance; rung 1 ships from the first serve and the decision record states the first round is measured on a proxy. Holdout membership is a write-time boolean benchmark_holdout computed at insert as an FNV-1a hash of (user_id, content_kind, item_id) at a 20% rate, with aggregates using WHERE NOT benchmark_holdout and benchmark exports WHERE benchmark_holdout. The flag filters but never becomes the label (that is the verdict table), and rotating the pseudonym would flip the split, so the key is frozen.

query: A team wants customer lifetime from order data in which many customers are still active. What goes wrong with naive averaging and with a single pooled Markov chain, and what fixes each?
expected_answer: Survival analysis handles censoring: averaging only customers who left gave 212.8 days and counting censored customers as left gave 250.9, against a true mean of 401.8, whereas Kaplan-Meier uses the censored customers properly. For value, a Markov chain with churn as an absorbing state values a new customer through (I - Q)^-1, but a single pooled chain gave 430.73 against a true 513.29 (about 19% low) because customers differ and the Markov property fails (77% versus 52% staying active); per-type chains averaged 515.1 against 515.0. The two models are alternatives, one modelling time to churn and the other state-by-state value.

query: Before a model's confidence field is used as the thresholds in three-band routing, what has to be true of it, and what happened when one such field was audited?
expected_answer: Three-band routing sets two thresholds per category from the cost of each error type, uses override rate, escalation rate and queue depth as monitors, and treats every human verdict as a label. That presumes the score is a probability. The audited 'confidence' (weight 0.15) was a fixed lookup on a 3-4 value enrichment_status, a status string dressed as a float; calibration needs a real probability, a reader that acts on it and independent labels. The probe's tag confidence was graded only against the same call's evidence_sufficient bit so it was registered UNGATED, and 'low confidence then escalate' stays unsafe until calibrated (ECE 0.106, Brier 0.130 on 982 raw tags).

query: What does a host rollback not undo, which invariants make code-only rollback safe, and how do build-state markers protect against trusting a stale READY status?
expected_answer: A host rollback restores code only, never migrations, rows or schedules, so the runbook says that first and rests on invariants: a deploy never applies a migration, never runs ingestion, enrichment or publishing, never enables a schedule, and promotion needs CI green on the exact SHA (checked with gh run list --json headSha,conclusion). Build-state markers (BUILT, ABSENT, UNVERIFIED, SPECIFIED for greenfield) are verified against the tree rather than inherited: six of eight inherited markers were wrong, a false BUILT is worse than a false ABSENT, and an earlier promotion plan had reached READY and was never executed.

query: If answer quality drops, how do operational metrics help locate the cause, and which traces should be sampled for scoring in production?
expected_answer: Latency, error rate, token usage and retrieval recall are health metrics orthogonal to the eval ladder; a quality regression with flat operations points at the model or prompt, while one accompanied by latency or error spikes points at infrastructure. For online scoring, 10-20% of traces are chosen by rule: negative feedback, high-cost dialogues (cost is a proxy for thrashing), a time window as a control group for normal traffic, and a full 48-hour review after a change. Manual labelling calibrates and an LLM judge gives breadth; using only the judge layer drifts.

query: In an eval CI that separates running from asserting, why is an overall improvement not enough to pass, and which rules and counting conventions catch hidden regressions?
expected_answer: The slow RUN phase writes results.jsonl and the fast ASSERT phase computes confidence intervals per slice against a baseline, with rule types including an absolute floor, a baseline-relative paired difference, a per-slice floor (no slice drops more than 10 points), an efficiency budget (cost per success within 1.2x baseline) and a regression set. This matters because slicing can hide losses: Billing +8, How-to +1 and Non-English -17 netted to an overall +1. Errors and refusals must count as failures or be reported as their own rate, since dropping the 8% of tasks on which system B errored creates a sample ratio mismatch; infra failures are retried and counted separately.

query: Why would a scaffold maintainer make a capability such as the checkpointer a template default instead of an opt-in, and what makes the opt-in alternative workable?
expected_answer: Template floor-raising prioritises scaffold additions by cross-portfolio gap frequency and 'removes the activation energy' (for example 0/5 repos had OTel spans), so the checkpointer should be a default, not an opt-in skill. The counter-case is Copier re-entry: .copier-answers.yml is durable scaffold state, and changing an answer through copier (clean git tree first, then copier update -d) is the only way a component enters after genesis, since hand-copied files silently fork. That add-later guarantee is what makes a minimal MVP scaffold credible, which is why the floor-raising page lists it as contradicting the default-everything approach.

query: In a Deep Agents harness, how do you persist memory across threads, and what design decision prevents one user's memories leaking into another's?
expected_answer: StateBackend is thread-scoped and the default, while StoreBackend persists across threads, needs store= and should use AsyncPostgresStore in production; a CompositeBackend routes by longest prefix, for example /memories/ to the StoreBackend (a path like /prefs.txt does not match it). Underneath is LangGraph's BaseStore, a cross-thread key-value store with optional vector search and explicit get/put, unlike the automatic single-thread checkpointer. Its key design decision is the namespace, such as (user_id, memory_type), because a wrong namespace leaks memories across users.

query: Which distribution would you use to model order value, and how should a single huge order change the choice of test when comparing groups?
expected_answer: Order value is modelled as lognormal, whose mean grows with sigma, while goodness-of-fit tests such as KS will reject any model given enough rows. For comparing groups, Welch is the default, but one 60,000 whale moved the Welch p-value from 0.165 to 0.506 whereas Mann-Whitney moved from 0.125 to 0.163. Mann-Whitney answers 'tends to be higher', not 'total revenue differs', so choose the test for the question and check design first (pairing, clustering, multiple comparisons).

query: A frozen router's PSI stays at 0.001 yet its error on automatically paid cases rises. What kind of drift is this, and how can it be detected?
expected_answer: It is concept drift, such as a new fraud type: in the router experiment PSI stayed at 0.001 while error on paid cases rose from 0.014 to 0.033 and cost to 5.181 (4.747 after recalibration, with error still 2.9%). PSI bins deciles of the score or inputs (thresholds: under 0.10 little shift, over 0.25 significant), needs no outcomes and ignores error rates, so it caught covariate drift (PSI 0.251, paid share 0.602 to 0.385, error unchanged at 0.014) but not this. Only labels on automatically paid cases reveal concept drift, hence a random audit sample.

query: What retry mechanisms exist in the Librarian CRAG pipeline and its LLM calls, and how should they be kept from compounding?
expected_answer: The CRAG gate compares the reranker confidence_score to 0.3 and a retry re-enters at retrieve with max retries 1 (about 400ms); confidence_threshold=0.0 disables it, and it is one of three thresholds (0.3 reranker score, 0.5 per-chunk grade, 0.7 whole-retrieval grade). Separately the Anthropic client should use max_retries=3, and a manual loop of 5 must not be stacked on the SDK's 3 because that makes 15 calls. The hardening list also surfaces an escalate signal in the API response so the caller sees when the retried answer is still not confident.

query: Which tier of a telemetry dashboard tends to go dark, and what check must a number pass before it is allowed to drive a behaviour change?
expected_answer: Tier 0 outcomes (task success, cost per merged PR) were dark while Tier 2-3 numbers such as a 97% cache hit rate and the compaction rate were tuned because they are easy to instrument; the action test is 'what would I do differently if this number changed?', and a pilot of about 20 hand-tagged sessions can light the tier. Before a number drives action it must pass the claim-verification gate: recompute it from the raw transcripts, count the right unit, establish the denominator and test causal direction, giving a verdict of CONFIRMED, OVERSTATED, INVERTED, PHANTOM or UNMEASURABLE. A failing claim cannot become a behaviour change, and the loop is propose-only.

query: A 90-day repeat rate fell from 31.6% to 20.2%. How do you separate 'every customer got worse' from 'we bought different customers', and what must hold for the cohorts being compared?
expected_answer: Rate and mix decomposition splits the 11.4-point fall into a rate effect (-6.2, every channel worse by 5-9 points) and a mix effect (-5.2, as a low-repeat channel grew from about 27.5% to 53.8% of new customers). The split depends on order, since reversing it gave -5.6 for mix and -5.8 for rates, so report it as about half and half, and it does not prove cause. The cohort triangle supplies the precondition: compare at fixed age and use only customers whose full 90-day window has completed, because filling an unreached cell with a partial figure reports a collapse.

query: Why did a venue backfill have to be paired with a fix to the ingestion path before standing places could be served through the event ranker, and which ranker rules would otherwise misbehave?
expected_answer: The migration backfilled venue_id on all 37 hospitality rows, but the single-page ingestion path had no venue field, so the next hand-added bar would reproduce the defect; the forward gap was made a required step of the same phase and the serving phase was gated on it. Widening the event type to standing content creates two hazards: the diversity ledger's venue-repetition cap returns 'no limit' on a null key, so three bars from one place would pass, and the junk-title filter (title equals venue name) would be true by construction for backfilled bars and exclude 100% of them. The fix is to scope that clause, and the missing_display_data check, to content_kind of event.

query: How do the graph explorer's chat agent and the five-agent Librarian RAG pipeline each signal that an answer may not be trustworthy?
expected_answer: The graph explorer's chat agent is a plain Anthropic tool-use loop (search_wiki and read_page, up to 8 turns) that computes grounding instead of trusting it: it emits cited, pages_read and ungrounded = cited minus pages_read, and cited ids are never added to the highlight set. The RAG pipeline's CRAG gate treats a confidence_score below 0.3 as fallback_requested and retries, after max_crag_retries (default 1) it generates from whatever is available, and escalate = not confident or fallback_requested is surfaced in the API response. One checks citations against pages actually read, the other checks retrieval score.

query: Why does a clean result from a contracts review not mean a diff is safe, and why should other review dimensions cite the contract too?
expected_answer: A contracts reporter returning [] shows only that no written rule was broken: the contract declared no dependency budget, a lint rule lived in CLAUDE.md rather than the contract, and an accessibility invariant was scoped to two files, so a clean verdict was an absent control rather than a satisfied one. Across 238 review findings, those anchored to a contract entry were fixed 9 of 9, other findings averaged 65% and the intent dimension 44%. Yet only 4% were anchored because only the contracts dimension cited the contract, so a contract_ref field on every finding lets all dimensions cite it, and gaps found this way are candidates for amending the contract.

query: Radix's dialog was adopted for four behaviours. Which one went untested, and why did a focus-restore test still pass while real dialogs dropped focus?
expected_answer: The hand-rolled dialogs lacked a focus trap, Escape to close, focus restore and scroll lock; the tests covered three, and focus restore, the one most likely to regress silently on a library upgrade, had none. A later component test 'restores focus to the trigger on close' stayed green because its fixture used the uncontrolled Dialog.Trigger, the only shape where Radix restores focus itself. Every dialog in the app was controlled, so triggerRef was null, onCloseAutoFocus prevented the default and focused nothing, and focus fell to body; a Playwright journey using the real components caught it, and the fix captures document.activeElement on open.

query: A volunteer team has only a weekend and wants a chatbot over a complex system. Which archetype can they realistically choose, and how far up the orchestration ladder should they go?
expected_answer: Conversational Interface is the semester-floor archetype (it alone needs auth, per-user scoping, history, tool-calling, deployment and evaluation), so a weekend team cannot choose it and should reframe toward Document Generation, the only weekend-sprint archetype. In the orchestration decision shortcut a weekend maps to a single prompt, and the governing bias is to start simple and escalate only on demonstrated need, since each pattern's limits are the next one's entry condition. The time budget is a hard constraint that interacts with the archetype's complexity floor.
